data.title: Impetigo — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Impetigo** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. What is impetigo and what are its types?**
- Contagious superficial (subcorneal) bacterial infection of the epidermis, commonest in children
- Non-bullous impetigo (impetigo contagiosa, ~70%): S. aureus (most), Streptococcus pyogenes; honey-coloured crusts
- Bullous impetigo: S. aureus phage group II (type 71) producing exfoliative toxins A and B that cleave desmoglein 1
- Ecthyma is the deeper (ulcerative) form

**Q2. Why are the crusts honey-coloured?**
- Dried serum from ruptured thin-roofed vesicopustules

**Q3. Where is the split in bullous impetigo and why?**
- Subcorneal/granular layer — exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 (same target as pemphigus foliaceus and SSSS)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis?**
- Non-bullous: eczema herpeticum/herpes simplex, impetiginised eczema, tinea faciei, scabies with pyoderma, pemphigus foliaceus, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Bullous: bullous insect bite, chronic bullous disease of childhood, bullous pemphigoid, thermal burn, bullous fixed drug eruption, SSSS, bullous erythema multiforme

**Q5. What is primary vs secondary impetigo (impetiginisation)?**
- Primary — on normal skin; secondary — on pre-existing dermatoses (eczema, scabies, pediculosis, insect bites, varicella)

**Q6. Does impetigo scar?**
- No — it is superficial; may leave temporary hypo/hyperpigmentation; ecthyma scars

**Q7. Complications?**
- Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (nephritogenic strains — not prevented by antibiotics); rheumatic fever is not associated with skin infection
- Cellulitis, lymphangitis, SSSS, sepsis, guttate psoriasis, scarlet fever

**Q8. How will you investigate?**
- Usually clinical; Gram stain (Gram-positive cocci in clusters/chains) and pus culture with sensitivity in recurrent/extensive cases or suspected MRSA
- Urine for haematuria/proteinuria if streptococcal (PSGN watch)

**Q9. Treatment of localised impetigo?**
- Remove crusts with soaks; topical mupirocin 2% or fusidic acid 2% three times daily for 5–7 days (ozenoxacin 1% twice daily for 5 days, retapamulin)

**Q10. Treatment of extensive impetigo or bullous impetigo?**
- Oral antibiotics for 7 days: cloxacillin/flucloxacillin, cephalexin/cefadroxil, amoxicillin–clavulanate; macrolide or clindamycin in penicillin allergy; co-trimoxazole/doxycycline for MRSA (age >8 for doxycycline)

**Q11. What is 'impetigo of Bockhart'?**
- Superficial staphylococcal folliculitis — small follicular pustules (not true impetigo)

**Q12. How will you prevent recurrence?**
- Treat the underlying dermatosis, nasal carriage (mupirocin 5 days), hygiene, separate towels, exclude from school until 24–48 h after starting antibiotics or lesions crusted

## Quick spotter facts
- Honey-coloured crusts on face around nose/mouth in a child
- Flaccid bullae with a hypopyon sign — bullous impetigo

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Bacterial infections); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.15. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
